```{r setup}
library(knitr)

# ---- Planning unit prices (USD per sample). EDIT THESE when the ALS quote arrives. ----
price <- c(
  pkg_A = 45,    # Cl by IC (EPA 300.0) + alkalinity
  pkg_B = 135,   # A + SO4, F, Br (IC), Na, K, Ca, Mg, B, Li, Si (ICP), TDS
  pkg_C = 225,   # B + ICP-MS trace-element suite (ME-MS14L type, as used on the 2026 field samples)
  iso   = 40     # delta-18O / delta-D, outside stable-isotope lab (not ALS)
)
qa_frac <- 0.10  # field duplicates and blanks, as a fraction of routine samples

tiers <- data.frame(
  tier = c("Lean", "Recommended", "Full"),
  intensive = c(10, 14, 28),     # daily samples, 2 sites (5, 7 or 14 days)
  monthly   = c(10, 24, 24),     # SBRR + SBGG, 5 or 12 months
  events    = c(0, 2, 8),        # storm / snowmelt samples, 2 sites
  extra     = c(0, 0, 12),       # SBW_0001/0002 and fissure, quarterly
  iso       = c(4, 8, 16),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
tiers$routine <- with(tiers, intensive + monthly + events + extra)
tiers$qa <- ceiling(tiers$routine * qa_frac)
tiers$total <- tiers$routine + tiers$qa

cost <- function(n, p, iso_n) n * p + iso_n * price[["iso"]]
tiers$A <- cost(tiers$total, price[["pkg_A"]], tiers$iso)
tiers$B <- cost(tiers$total, price[["pkg_B"]], tiers$iso)
tiers$C <- cost(tiers$total, price[["pkg_C"]], tiers$iso)
usd <- function(x) paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ","))
```

## Summary

I am calibrating continuous specific conductance from two in-stream loggers (SBRR at Rhodes Road above the thermal inflow, and SBGG at Geiger Grade below it) against laboratory chloride. **Method:** paired grab samples bracket logger readings; chloride (and major ions, alkalinity, field pH/temperature/conductance) is measured at the lab, and I fit time-aware models (linear, GAM, random forest) validated with rolling-origin cross-validation. **Application:** the calibrated record gives continuous chloride flux, which is the standard tracer for thermal-water discharge at Steamboat (Sorey and Spielman 2008, 2017). It lets us ask whether the 2025 Lower Sinter Terrace eruption changed outflow, and it replaces the sparse, expensive chemistry that has limited the discharge record. **Reasoning:** a Monte Carlo test on the real logger record (with the days the loggers sat in open air removed) shows daily sampling gives a reconstruction error of about 3-4% of mean conductance, while biweekly sampling gives about 8-10%, and 7-13% depending on the start day, so a short intensive window followed by monthly samples across a full year captures both fast variability and seasonal stability. **Hypothesis:** one site-specific relationship between conductance and chloride holds through the year, with deviations during storms and snowmelt from dilution. **Value:** once calibrated, the loggers give a continuous chloride and thermal-discharge record for a small fraction of the cost of regular chemistry, and the same samples provide the end-member chemistry for the mixing and reactive-transport work.

## Sampling plan

| Phase | Sites | Cadence and timing | What is measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intensive calibration | SBRR, SBGG | Daily (or sub-daily) for 5, 7 or 14 days; start fall/winter 2026 | Cl, anions, cations, alkalinity (package set below); field pH, temperature, conductance |
| Monthly seasonal sampling | SBRR, SBGG | Once a month for 5 or 12 months after the intensive window | Same package |
| Storm / snowmelt | SBRR, SBGG | 1 to 4 events, 2 samples per event | Same package |
| Extra sites (Full tier only) | SBW_0001, SBW_0002, active fissure (access permitting) | Quarterly | Same package |
| Isotopes | SBRR, SBGG (subset) | About one sample per site per season with a regular visit | delta-18O, delta-D |
| QA | All | 10% duplicates and blanks | Same package |

```{r rec}
rec <- tiers[tiers$tier == "Recommended", ]
```

**Recommended option:** the Recommended tier with package B, about `r rec$total` chemistry samples and `r rec$iso` isotope samples, roughly `r usd(rec$B)` for the year. It is the smallest design that covers a full seasonal cycle at both stations, includes the ions needed for the mixing-model cross-check, and keeps the daily window short enough to be done in the field by one person. The Lean tier gives a first calibration but no seasonal test; the Full tier adds the fissure and resort wells and a longer daily window, and depends on Ormat access.

**Notes for the cost discussion.** (1) ALS lab pricing depends on method set, turnaround time and any UNR or project discount, so the totals above scale directly with the package prices in Table 2. (2) Shipping, sample bottles, filters and sampling supplies are not included. (3) Tier totals can be reduced by running packages A or B on routine samples and C only on the quarterly subset.

## Equations used for the conductance proxy, model fitting and sampling-error test

**1. Specific conductance from logger conductivity.** The loggers record raw electrical conductivity $EC$ at water temperature $T$ (degrees C). I remove the temperature effect with the USGS non-linear compensation (coefficient $a = 0.0191$ per degree C, to be recalibrated against field checks):

$$SC_{25} = \frac{EC}{1 + a\,(T - 25)}$$

**2. Chloride from specific conductance (the proxy).** Chloride is the conservative tracer of thermal water, and in this system conductance tracks chloride because chloride and sodium dominate the thermal fluid. The simplest model is a linear regression, fitted to paired samples:

$$\mathrm{Cl}_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,SC_{25,t} + \varepsilon_t$$

The generalized additive model (GAM) adds smooth terms for conductance and temperature and a seasonal harmonic ($d$ is day of year; splines with $k = 4$):

$$\mathrm{Cl}_t = \beta_0 + f_1(SC_{25,t}) + f_2(T_t) + \beta_3 \sin\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi d_t}{365}\right) + \beta_4 \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi d_t}{365}\right) + \varepsilon_t$$

A random forest on the same predictors is the skill benchmark. Models are scored with rolling-origin (blocked, time-aware) cross-validation: each fold trains on all samples up to time $t_k$ and predicts the next block, so autocorrelation cannot inflate skill:

$$\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{Cl}_i - \widehat{\mathrm{Cl}}_i\right)^2}$$

**3. Monte Carlo sampling-interval test.** For a candidate sampling interval of $f$ days and a logger step of $\Delta t$ minutes, the number of logger steps between samples is $n_f = f \cdot 1440 / \Delta t$. For draw $j = 1,\dots,200$ a random start offset $o_j \sim \mathrm{U}\{1,\dots,n_f\}$ selects samples at steps $o_j, o_j + n_f, o_j + 2n_f, \dots$. The full series is rebuilt by linear interpolation between those samples, and the error against the dense record $y_t$ is

$$\mathrm{RMSE}_{f,j} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\left(y_t - \hat y_{t}^{(f,j)}\right)^2},\qquad \text{reported as } 100\,\frac{\overline{\mathrm{RMSE}_{f}}}{\bar y}\ \text{percent of the mean.}$$

**4. Chloride flux and thermal discharge.** With discharge $Q$ and concentration $C$, chloride mass flux is the integral of $C\,Q$, computed by the trapezoid rule; the thermal-water inflow between SBRR (upstream) and SBBV (downstream) uses an end-member chloride $C_{TW} = 820$ mg/L (Sorey and Colvard 1992):

$$M = \int C(t)\,Q(t)\,dt,\qquad Q_{TW} = \frac{Q_{BV}\,C_{BV} - Q_{RR}\,C_{RR}}{C_{TW}}$$

## Conductivity record and the data each analysis uses

```{r data}
find_root <- function(p = getwd()) { for (i in 1:5) { if (file.exists(file.path(p, "database", "geochem_operational.sqlite"))) return(p); p <- dirname(p) }; stop("project root not found") }
root <- find_root()
library(DBI); library(RSQLite); library(ggplot2); library(dplyr)
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), file.path(root, "database", "geochem_operational.sqlite"), flags = SQLITE_RO)
ec <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT l.external_station_code AS site, o.timestamp, o.sc_25c, o.qc_flag
  FROM Conductivity_Observations o
  JOIN Conductivity_Loggers cl ON o.logger_id = cl.logger_id
  JOIN Locations l ON cl.location_id = l.location_id
  WHERE l.external_station_code IN ('SBRR','SBGG') AND o.sc_25c IS NOT NULL")
ec$timestamp <- as.POSIXct(ec$timestamp, tz = "UTC")
ec$site <- factor(ec$site, c("SBRR", "SBGG"), c("SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream)", "SBGG (Geiger Grade, downstream)"))
ec$use <- ifelse(is.na(ec$qc_flag), "Used in Monte Carlo", "QC-flagged, excluded")
```

```{r fig-record}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
old_wd <- setwd(root); suppressMessages(source('scripts/analysis/sampling_frequency/06_monte_carlo_air_exclusion.R')); setwd(old_wd)
raw <- get_sc_record(con)
rt <- retrieval_times(raw)
ec <- raw
ec$class <- ifelse(!is.na(ec$qc_flag), 'QC-flagged, excluded', 'Used in Monte Carlo')
for (i in seq_len(nrow(rt))) ec$class[ec$site == rt$site[i] & is.na(ec$qc_flag) & ec$timestamp >= rt$t[i] - 3*86400 & ec$timestamp <= rt$t[i] + 3600] <- 'Open-air days, excluded'
ec$class[ec$site == 'SBGG' & is.na(ec$qc_flag) & ec$timestamp >= as.POSIXct('2026-09-29', tz = 'UTC')] <- 'Open-air days, excluded'
ec$class <- factor(ec$class, c('Used in Monte Carlo', 'Open-air days, excluded', 'QC-flagged, excluded'))
ec$site <- factor(ec$site, c('SBRR','SBGG'), c('SBRR (Rhodes Road, upstream)', 'SBGG (Geiger Grade, downstream)'))
cols <- c('Used in Monte Carlo' = '#0072B2', 'Open-air days, excluded' = '#999999', 'QC-flagged, excluded' = '#D55E00')
ggplot(ec, aes(timestamp, sc_25c, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.25, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~site, ncol = 1, scales = 'free_y') +
  scale_color_manual(NULL, values = cols) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2, alpha = 1))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = 'Specific conductance (uS/cm, 25 C)',
       title = 'Logger record used for the Monte Carlo sampling-interval test',
       subtitle = paste0(format(sum(ec$class == 'Used in Monte Carlo'), big.mark = ','), ' readings used; ', format(sum(ec$class == 'Open-air days, excluded'), big.mark = ','), ' open-air readings and ', sum(ec$class == 'QC-flagged, excluded'), ' QC-flagged readings excluded'),
       caption = 'Open-air days: the 3 days before each retrieval (both loggers) and SBGG from 2026-09-29, when it began to be exposed to air\n(daily temperature range rises from about 5 to 7-8 C). The Monte Carlo test subsamples the blue record at 1, 2, 3, 7 and 14 days\nand rebuilds it by interpolation (equation 3).') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(legend.position = 'bottom', plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0))
```

Mean error rises from about 3-4%% of mean conductance with daily samples to about 8-10%% at 14 days.](%s)\n", f))

## What the GAM has and has not been run on

The sampling interval in this plan comes from the Monte Carlo test on the **real** logger record (Figures 1 and 3). The chloride models themselves, including the GAM, have **not** been fitted to real paired data, because no chloride sample yet overlaps the logger record (zero pairs). They have been run only as a code test on a simulated data set (`simulate_synthetic_pairs()` in `03_chloride_models.R`): 60 samples every three days from 1 May 2026, with

$$SC = 300 + 40\sin\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi d}{365}\right) + \mathrm{N}(0,15),\quad T = 15 + 8\sin\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi (d-60)}{365}\right) + \mathrm{N}(0,1.5),$$

$$\mathrm{Cl} = 1 + 0.071\,SC_{\text{lag}} + 0.1\,T_{\text{lag}} + \mathrm{N}(0,1.5),$$

where the lag is six days. The slope 0.071 comes from the single real SBRR pair (Cl 17.1 mg/L at 241 uS/cm on 2026-05-01), so the simulated chloride stays in a realistic range; every other value is made up. Because the data were generated from a known linear rule, the exercise shows only that the fitting and cross-validation code runs and recovers a known relationship. It does not show how well a GAM will perform on Steamboat Creek, and it did not influence the sampling interval. The only real fit is the linear regression on 181 historical NDEP pairs in Figure 2, which predates the loggers. The calibration samples proposed in this document supply the first real pairs for the GAM.
